newsitem.title: KENYA: U.N. has new fears over safety of Rwandan refugees.
newsitem.headline: U.N. has new fears over safety of Rwandan refugees.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR expressed new fears on Monday for thousands of Rwandan Hutus in former Zaire, saying it had strong concerns for their security.

"We are worried about the safety of the refugees we know about and obviously very concerned about the ones we cannot reach," said Peter Kessler, a UNHCR spokesman in Kisangani in the northwest of the new Democratic Republic of Congo.

Kessler said UNHCR officials at the weekend for the first time had been able to travel farther than 42 km (25 miles) south of Kisangani in an attempt to locate thousands of refugees who fled their makeshift camps at Biaro and Kasese in April.
They reached a point 48 km (27 miles) south before being turned back by soldiers who said the rest of the route was mined.
"We saw no refugees but local Zaireans said they had seen some beyond kilometre 48," Kessler said. "There were a lot of soldiers on the road, however."
Biaro and Kasese, makeshift sites for nearly 85,000 Hutu refugees, emptied on April 21 after attacks by local villagers and then rebel soldiers before a U.N. airlift to take them back to Rwanda.
More than 35,000 drifted back and have since been flown home, but aid officials have no idea where the rest might be and Congo and Rwandan officials deny such large numbers exist.
Fears for the refugees increased following evidence of massacres earlier this month by rebel soldiers at Mbandaka, about 500 kms (300 miles) further west.

Witnesses told Reuters rebel soldiers killed over 300 unarmed refugees at Mbandaka days before Kinshasha fell to the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL) lead by Laurent Kabila, who declared himself president.
Residents in Kisangani have also told of hundreds, possibly thousands of those who fled Biaro being butchered and their bodies burned at a point 52 km (32 miles) south of the city.

Kabila has strongly denied his forces had any role in massacres, but warned that those who commit atrocities would be punished. More than 1.5 million Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 to escape reprisal for the genocide of up to 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Most returned when Kabila's forces began their offensive at the end of last year, but more than 300,000 others -- including a hard core of former Rwandan Hutu soldiers and Interahamwe militiamen and their familes -- fled farther west.
With more than 35,000 refugees now airlifted home from Kisangani, UNHCR officials are focusing their attention on Mbandaka and the dense jungle between Ubundu and Kisangani.

Nearly 3,000 refugees remain at Ubilo, 80 km (50 miles) south of Kisangani, and officials report the number rising by around 50-60 a day. The UNHCR is also trying to reach over 25,000 refugees who were reported to have walked through Ikela, 230 km (140 miles) southwest of Kisangani, last month.
